title: At the Omni Parker House, rumors of paranormal activity stretch generations

content:
The exterior signage of Omni Parker House Oct. 24. The hotel first opened in 1855 during Boston’s golden age.

Few places represent Boston’s old-world charm better than the Omni Parker House hotel, which neighbors the Common and is one of the city’s most iconic and most haunted locations. Standing 15 stories high and boasting stores lined with gold trim, the hotel signifies the pathway from old-world Boston to modern-day.

But despite its charming aesthetics, the hotel has earned a reputation for paranormal activity. Built in 1855 by Harvey Parker, the Omni Parker House stands along the Freedom Trail. The hotel opened during Boston’s “golden age,” when many European immigrants chose to make the city their home.

Since its opening, history has unfolded in the hotel. Future Vietnamese communist leader Ho Chi Minh and civil rights activist Malcolm X both reportedly worked in the same kitchen, where they helped perfect its now-famous Boston cream pie. John F. Kennedy proposed to Jacqueline Bouvier at a table in the hotel’s dining room. Charles Dickens roomed for about five months during the height of his literary career, hosting readings of his most famous works for anyone who wanted to hear.

“It’s one of the most important hotels in the whole country,” said Susan Wilson, the Parker House historian for the past 20 years.

But the Parker House is associated with more than memories of baking and marriage. The hotel is also the site of numerous unexplained paranormal events, with much of it tied to the multiple people who reportedly died in the building.

One of the most haunted locations in the hotel is the 10th floor, where the spirit of Harvey Parker, who founded the hotel, is said to linger. With his proud mustache and heavy-set build, Parker is said to continue checking over the guests on the floor, much as he did back in the 1800s. Guests report seeing his shadowy figure in the hallways of the floor, some even claiming to see his presence standing at the foot of their bed, surveying their room.

Vinh Trinh, who visited Boston back in 2025 with his husband, experienced firsthand what he thinks might be a paranormal experience while staying on the 10th floor.

“I constantly smelled cigarette smoke. I just couldn’t get rid of it and smoking [on the floor] wasn’t allowed,” Trinh said. “But then the lights started flickering in my room … It was late, so I just went to bed. When my husband came in to check on me, the lights started flickering again.”

Before Trinh got to their hotel room, his husband, who was already staying on the 10th floor, woke up in the middle of the night to the sound of a fire alarm that appeared to only blare in his room. When he asked someone at the concierge desk the next morning whether the alarm was meant to go off, the concierge responded that there was no record of the alarm ever sounding in the first place.

Trinh did not consider the paranormal being a possible explanation for the activity until a waiter at a nearby restaurant overheard a conversation between him and his partner and informed the couple of the hotel’s haunted reputation. 

“I think in the beginning, I was just very logical about it, trying to figure out what’s happening,” Trinh said. “The paranormal activity itself didn’t really occur to us until the restaurant owner was like ‘No, this place is like actually haunted.’”

On a historical tour of the hotel late October 2026 led by Wilson, all 10 Parker House guests who attended reported some activity they deemed paranormal. From flickering lights, the constant smell of cigarettes and shadows in the corners of their eyes, the majority of the activity seemed to occur on the third floor and Room 303.

Wilson said in the mid-20th century, a man known for heavy drinking and cigarette smoking died in Room 303. To this day, guests report smelling alcohol or cigarettes when staying on the floor, and elevators in the hotel will take guests to the third floor even when they push a different button.

Kelly Briggs, a guest at the hotel visiting from Wisconsin with her child, did not believe in paranormal activity until a few days into her stay.

“We were just messing around yesterday, trying to find the haunted places, and we went to Room 303. We found it, took a selfie and later, when we went back to our room, we pulled the picture back up and the room number was not there. The horse [above the engraved room number] was there, but no room number,” Briggs said.

Wilson herself has never experienced anything paranormal but remains open-minded to the possibility that the hotel is, in fact, haunted. And as a city older than the country’s independence, Boston has a deep appreciation for the antique. The Omni Parker House isn’t just a well-known site for spotting ghosts; it’s a place to experience the past. Nothing shows this more than the Parker House’s historical gallery, which displays the hotel door to Charles Dickens’ room and the hotel’s original keys from the 1800s. 

“There is a great deal of evidence that paranormal activity has occurred here. Luckily, it’s all very friendly,” Wilson said. “I think it’s a big deal because, if they weren’t [friendly], I know that would scare people away. But it seems that there are way more people who are enticed by that and think, ‘I’d like to participate in this,’ particularly because it is a friendly atmosphere.”
